{{short description|Geometrical construction based on extending the sides of a triangle}}
{{Use dmy dates|date = May 2020}}

[[File:Conway circle theorem.svg|thumb|upright=1.37|A [[triangle]]'s [[John Horton Conway|Conway]] [[circle]] with its six [[Concentric objects|concentric]] points (solid black), the triangle's [[Incircle and excircles of a triangle|incircle]] (dashed gray), and the centre of both circles (white); solid and dashed [[line segment]]s of the same colour are equal in length|alt=A geometrical diagram showing a circle inside a triangle inside a larger circle.]]

In [[Euclidean geometry|plane geometry]], the '''Conway circle theorem''' states that when the sides meeting at each [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]] of a [[triangle]] are extended by the length of the opposite side, the six endpoints of the three resulting [[line segment]]s lie on a [[circle]] whose centre is the [[incentre]] of the triangle. The circle on which these six points lie is called the '''Conway circle''' of the triangle.<ref>{{Cite web|title=John Horton Conway|url=http://www.cardcolm.org/JHC.html|last=|first=|date=|website=www.cardcolm.org|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200520084537/http://www.cardcolm.org/JHC.html |archive-date=20 May 2020 |access-date=29 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{mathworld|title=Conway Circle|urlname=ConwayCircle|access-date=29 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="FJGC">{{cite journal|title = A Generalization of the Conway Circle | author = Francisco Javier García Capitán|journal = Forum Geometricorum| volume = 13 | year = 2013 | pages = 191–195 | url=http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2013volume13/FG2013volume13.pdf#page=195}}</ref>  The theorem and circle are named after mathematician [[John Horton Conway]].

== Proof ==
[[File:Conway circle theorem proof.svg|thumb|upright=1.37|segments of equal color are of equal length <math>\begin{align}\triangle IF_cP_a &\cong \triangle IF_cQ_b \cong \triangle IF_aP_b \\ &\cong \triangle IF_aQ_c \cong \triangle IF_bP_c \\ &\cong \triangle IF_bQ_a \\ \Rightarrow \, |IP_a|&=|IQ_a|=|IP_b|=|IQ_b|\\ &=|IP_c|=|IQ_c| \end{align}</math>]]
Let ''I'' be the center of the [[incircle]] of triangle ''ABC'', ''r'' its radius and ''F<sub>a</sub>'',  ''F<sub>b</sub>'' and  ''F<sub>c</sub>'' the three points where the incircle touches the triangle sides ''a'', ''b'' and ''c''. Since the (extended) triangle sides are [[Tangent lines to circles|tangents]] of the incircle it follows that ''IF<sub>a</sub>'', ''IF<sub>b</sub>'' and ''IF<sub>c</sub>'' are perpendicular to ''a'', ''b'' and ''c''. Furthermore, the following equalities for line segments hold. |AF<sub>c</sub>|=|AF<sub>b</sub>|, |BF<sub>c</sub>|=|BF<sub>a</sub>|, |CF<sub>a</sub>|=|CF<sub>b</sub>|. With that the six triangles ''IF<sub>c</sub>P<sub>a</sub>'', ''IF<sub>c</sub>Q<sub>b</sub>'', ''IF<sub>a</sub>P<sub>b</sub>'', ''IF<sub>a</sub>Q<sub>c</sub>'', ''IF<sub>b</sub>Q<sub>a</sub>'' and ''IF<sub>b</sub>P<sub>c</sub>'' all have a side of length |''AF<sub>c</sub>''|+|''BF<sub>c</sub>''|+|''CF<sub>a</sub>''| and a side of length ''r'' with a right angle between them. This means that due [[Congruence (geometry)#Congruence of triangles|SAS congruence theorem for triangles]] all six triangles are congruent, which yields |''IP<sub>a</sub>''|=|''IQ<sub>a</sub>''|=|''IP<sub>b</sub>''|=|''IQ<sub>b</sub>''|=|''IP<sub>c</sub>''|=|''IQ<sub>c</sub>''|. So the six points ''P<sub>a</sub>'', ''Q<sub>a</sub>'', ''P<sub>b</sub>'', ''Q<sub>b</sub>'', ''P<sub>c</sub>'' and ''Q<sub>c</sub>'' have all the same distance from the triangle incenter ''I'', that is they lie on a common circle with center ''I''.

== Additional properties ==
The radius of the Conway circle is
:<math>\sqrt{r^2 + s^2}=\sqrt{\frac{a^2b+ab^2+b^2c+bc^2+a^2c+ac^2+abc}{a+b+c}}</math>
where <math>r</math> and <math>s</math> are the inradius and semiperimeter of the triangle.<ref name="FJGC"/>

==Generalisation==
[[File:Side divider theorem2a.svg|thumb|upright=1.37|Conway's circle theorem as a special case of the generalisation, called "side divider theorem" (Villiers) or "windscreen wiper theorem" (Polster))]]
Conway's circle is a special case of a more general circle for a triangle that can be obtained as follows: Given any △ABC with an arbitrary point P on line AB. Construct BQ = BP, CR = CQ, AS = AR, BT = BS, CU = CT. Then AU = AP, and PQRSTU is cyclic.<ref name="MdeV">{{cite journal|title = Conway's Circle Theorem as a Special Case of a More General Side Divider Theorem | author = Michael de Villiers|journal = Learning and Teaching Mathematics| number = 34 | year = 2023 | pages = 37–42 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/371806890}}</ref>

If you place P on the extended triangle side AB such that BP=b and BP being completely outside the triangle then the above constructions yield Conway's circle theorem.
